evidence.statement: The artifact accurately reflects the source: GPT-5 series capabilities include multimodal inputs, structured outputs, and tool use; the Foundry playground supports interactive image testing; the Responses API accepts text and image inputs; and Base64 converts binary image bytes to safe ASCII text. Source: 11. Get started with computer vision in Azure.md, sections “Multimodal models in Microsoft Foundry,” “Image analysis in the Foundry playground,” “Using the Azure OpenAI API for image analysis,” and the Base64 note.

Each item has one defensible answer under its instructions. The connection-settings question distinguishes the required key, endpoint, and deployment name from Base64 request content, while the model-family question distinguishes GPT-5 series from an API or playground.

Most distractors represent credible category confusions, such as testing versus coding, encoding versus credentials, and API versus playground. Some distractors are comparatively obvious category mismatches, especially “Foundry playground” and “OpenAI Responses API” as alternatives to a model family.

Wrong choices and incorrect true/false feedback diagnose realistic misconceptions: confusing the playground with code execution, Base64 with authentication, deployment identifiers with inputs, and a model family with an API.

The ordered session starts with the relatively advanced GPT-5 capability bundle, moves to the playground, repeats concepts in paired remembering/understanding items, and later returns to model, API, and encoding topics. Source sections “Multimodal models in Microsoft Foundry,” “Image analysis in the Foundry playground,” and “Using the Azure OpenAI API for image analysis” support a clearer progression from capability and interactive testing to a programmatic text-plus-image request.

The session uses only multiple-choice and true/false mechanics, arranged in repeated paired blocks: multiple-choice items, then true/false items, repeated three times. This creates predictable rhythm rather than natural variation.

Multiple-choice stems vary between “Which capabilities,” “What is,” “Which items,” “Which model family,” and “Which facts,” but the six true/false prompts rely heavily on repeated declarative patterns about whether a source claim is true or false.

The items are primarily decontextualized recall prompts. Apart from the generic connection-to-Python framing, they do not resemble concrete developer tasks such as attaching a customer photo and text prompt in an application, although the source provides such application examples.

Feedback is generally instructional: multiple-choice options include rationales, misconception labels, and better-fit guidance, while true/false items include intrinsic and instructional feedback. The briefest explanations, such as the playground explanation, could provide a more explicit next step.

The item metadata is explicitly Level 1, and most prompts are tagged Remembering or Understanding, which fits the stated introductory SLO to describe how text and image inputs are sent to a deployed model. The session does not require writing code or debugging an API request.

The artifact consistently distinguishes Foundry, playground, deployment name, Responses API, multimodal inputs, and Base64 in ways aligned with the source. “OpenAI-compatible APIs” is a broader paraphrase than the source’s “OpenAI API,” but it does not change the tested concept.

The session is source-faithful and provides useful misconception feedback, but the exact sequence feels repetitive, begins with a less foundational capability bundle, and offers little authentic application of the stated text-plus-image workflow. Source: 11. Get started with computer vision in Azure.md, multimodal models, playground, and Responses API sections.
